input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

Okay! Imagine you have a toy car, but it breaks. Your friend gives you a new toy car that works perfectly. You put your friend’s toy car in your toy box and play with it every day.

Now, your own toy cars are made by you, but your friend’s toy car was made by your friend. Over time, sometimes a tiny bit of your own toy pieces might stick to the new car, but most of the car is still your friend’s. Your body is a little like that.

If someone gets a new heart (or kidney, or liver) from another person, that new organ is made of the donor’s cells. Your body tries to help the new organ work by sending in some of your own cells, but most of the organ is still made of the donor’s cells. So, for the rest of that person’s life, most of the new organ’s cells are from the donor, not from them. But your body does its best to take care of the new organ and make it work well!
